sections.title: Describing appearance
sections.objective: Describe someone’s basic physical appearance respectfully and identify people.
sections.explanation: Use ser for general build/features, tener for hair/eyes and llevar for clothing or accessories currently worn.

examples.es: Es alto y tiene el pelo corto.
examples.en: He is tall and has short hair.

examples.es: Lleva gafas y una camisa azul.
examples.en: He/she is wearing glasses and a blue shirt.

examples.es: ¿Quién es la mujer de pelo rizado?
examples.en: Who is the woman with curly hair?

commonMistakes.explanation: Hair is normally described with tener.
Use the article and plural adjective.

practicePrompts.prompt: Describe two people in a photo without naming them.
Ask who someone is based on one visual feature.
Change a masculine description to feminine.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Adjust only forms that mark gender.

checkpoints: I can describe build, hair, eyes and clothing.
I can identify a person from a simple description.

sections.title: Describing personality
sections.objective: Describe personality and give a simple reason or contrast.
sections.explanation: Personality normally uses ser + adjective. Agreement still applies; many -e adjectives do not change for gender.

examples.en: I am quite calm but sociable.

examples.es: Parece serio, pero es muy simpático.
examples.en: He seems serious, but is very friendly.

commonMistakes.explanation: A general personality trait uses ser.
This adjective marks feminine with -a.

practicePrompts.prompt: Describe yourself using three adjectives and one contrast.
Describe two family members without repeating adjectives.
Sort adjectives into positive, neutral or context-dependent.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Meaning depends on context; justify one choice.

checkpoints: I can describe personality with varied adjectives.
I can connect two traits with y, pero or también.

sections.title: Family and relationships
sections.objective: Describe a simple family network and state relationships, names, ages and occupations.
sections.explanation: Use tener for family members and possessives to show relationships. Spanish kinship terms generally use an article or possessive.

reference.note: padres can mean parents; parientes means relatives, not parents.

examples.es: Tengo dos hijos y una hermana.
examples.en: I have two children and one sister.

examples.es: Carlos es el hermano de Marta.

commonMistakes.explanation: Parientes means relatives; padres means parents.
Do not combine a normal possessive adjective with an article.

practicePrompts.prompt: Describe your real or invented family in six sentences.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use at least four kinship words.

practicePrompts.prompt: Explain three relationships in a family tree.
Ask about siblings, children and relationship status politely.

checkpoints: I can explain who is who in a family.
I can ask and answer basic family questions.

sections.title: Gustar, encantar and interesar
sections.objective: Express and ask about likes, strong likes and interests with correct pronouns and verb agreement.
sections.explanation: The thing liked controls singular/plural agreement; the indirect-object pronoun identifies the experiencer. Use gusta with an infinitive or singular noun and gustan with plural nouns.

reference.negative: no goes before the pronoun: No me gusta.

examples.es: A Marta le interesa la historia.

commonMistakes.explanation: Plural things require gustan.
Use an indirect-object pronoun; the coffee is grammatically the subject.

practicePrompts.prompt: Make “Me gusta el museo” plural.
Ask five likes questions and record short answers.
State two likes, one strong like, one dislike and one interest.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use all three verbs and no.

checkpoints: I reliably choose gusta versus gustan.
I can use all six indirect-object pronouns in recognition and me/te/le/nos actively.

sections.title: Likes and leisure
sections.objective: Talk about free-time activities, frequency and preferences, and invite someone simply.
sections.explanation: Combine gustar-type verbs with activity infinitives and present-tense action verbs. Add frequency expressions to make answers conversational.

patterns.form: En mi tiempo libre + present verb
Normalmente / a veces / nunca + present verb

examples.es: Los fines de semana salgo con amigos.
examples.en: At weekends I go out with friends.

examples.es: Me gusta escuchar música mientras cocino.
examples.en: I like listening to music while I cook.
Sometimes we go to the cinema.
Do you want to have a drink this afternoon?

commonMistakes.explanation: After gusta, use the infinitive.
Avoid double placement of no and preverbal nunca.

practicePrompts.prompt: Speak for 45 seconds about your leisure time.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Include three activities and three frequencies.

practicePrompts.prompt: Ask what someone likes doing and when.
Invite someone to two activities and accept/decline.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: ¿Quieres…? Sí, vale. / Lo siento, no puedo.

checkpoints: I can describe my usual leisure activities.
I can ask about preferences and make a simple invitation.

sections.title: Present tense: irregular verbs
sections.objective: Use frequent stem-changing, first-person irregular and fully irregular verbs in conversation.
sections.explanation: Group irregulars by pattern: e→ie, o→ue, e→i, irregular yo forms, and unique verbs. Nosotros/vosotros usually do not stem-change.

examples.es: Empiezo a trabajar a las nueve.

examples.en: I hear music in the street.

commonMistakes.explanation: Nosotros normally keeps the infinitive stem.
Conocer has the yo form conozco.

practicePrompts.prompt: Sort ten verbs by e→ie, o→ue, e→i, irregular yo or unique.
Conjugate pensar, poder and pedir aloud.
Make five true sentences using five different irregular verbs.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Include at least one nosotros form.

checkpoints: I recognise the main irregular patterns.
I can actively use common yo, tú and nosotros forms.

sections.title: Reflexive verbs
sections.objective: Use reflexive pronouns with common daily-routine and personal-care verbs.
sections.explanation: A reflexive pronoun matches the subject and normally goes before a conjugated verb. The verb itself still conjugates normally or irregularly.

examples.en: What time do you go to bed?
I am going to get dressed.

commonMistakes.explanation: Use one reflexive pronoun before the conjugated verb.
The verb ending must also agree with nosotros.

practicePrompts.prompt: Conjugate levantarse in all six persons.
Change “Me ducho” to nosotros and ellos.
Describe a morning using four reflexive verbs.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Sequence with primero, después and luego.

checkpoints: I can match all reflexive pronouns to subjects.
I can use reflexive verbs before conjugated verbs and attached to infinitives.

sections.title: Daily routines and habits
sections.objective: Describe a normal day, sequence events and say when and how often they happen.
sections.explanation: Mix reflexive and non-reflexive verbs with time and frequency. Spanish uses a la/las for clock times and por la mañana/tarde/noche for parts of day.

examples.es: Me despierto a las seis y media.
examples.en: I wake up at half past six.
I work from nine to five.

examples.es: Después de cenar, veo la televisión.
Los viernes suelo trabajar en casa.
examples.en: On Fridays I usually work at home.

commonMistakes.explanation: Clock time uses a la/las.
Después de is followed by noun or infinitive.

practicePrompts.prompt: Create a six-event weekday timeline and narrate it.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Include exact times and sequence words.

practicePrompts.prompt: Compare your weekday and weekend routines.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use normalmente, pero and los fines de semana.

practicePrompts.prompt: Ask a partner five routine questions.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use ¿A qué hora…? and ¿Con qué frecuencia…?

checkpoints: I can narrate a typical day for one minute.
I can ask and answer about times and frequency.

sections.title: Possessive adjectives
sections.objective: Express ownership and family relationships using short-form possessives.
sections.explanation: Possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner. Mi, tu and su vary only for number; nuestro and vuestro vary for gender and number.

reference.disambiguation: Use de + person where su is unclear: la hermana de Ana.

examples.es: Mi hermano vive con sus hijos.
examples.en: My brother lives with his children.

commonMistakes.explanation: Nuestro agrees with the feminine plural noun casas.

commonMistakes.correct: el libro de Ana / su libro
commonMistakes.explanation: Use either de + person or a possessive, not both.

practicePrompts.prompt: Change “mi casa” to plural, then to “our houses”.
Choose su/sus/nuestro/nuestra for four nouns.
Describe five people or objects in your family/home using possessives.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Include mi, su and nuestro forms.

checkpoints: I can choose singular versus plural possessives.
I can disambiguate su with de + person.

sections.title: Quantifiers and amounts
sections.objective: Express approximate amounts with count and non-count nouns.
sections.explanation: Some quantifiers agree in gender and number; adverbial poco/mucho with verbs does not. Learn countable and uncountable examples.

examples.es: Hay muchos restaurantes en el centro.
examples.en: There are many restaurants in the centre.
I work a lot during the week.

commonMistakes.explanation: The quantifier agrees with feminine plural tiendas.
With a verb, mucho is an invariable adverb.

practicePrompts.prompt: Complete six noun phrases with the correct quantifier form.
Use poco/pocos and mucha/muchas in four sentences.
Describe what your town has a lot of and little of.

checkpoints: I can make quantifiers agree with nouns.
I distinguish mucho with a noun from mucho modifying a verb.

sections.title: Food and drink
sections.objective: Name common foods, express preferences and dietary needs, and discuss meals.
sections.explanation: Learn food in meal and shopping contexts rather than as isolated lists. Use tomar for food/drink in common meal expressions in Spain.

patterns.meaning: I am allergic to / I do not eat…

examples.es: Para desayunar tomo café y tostadas.
examples.en: For breakfast I have coffee and toast.

examples.es: Soy alérgica a los frutos secos.

commonMistakes.explanation: A stable allergy is normally expressed with ser.
Singular food noun takes gusta.

practicePrompts.prompt: Sort foods into meals or food groups, allowing overlaps.
Describe what you normally eat in a day.
Explain one dietary need to a server.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use no como, sin or soy alérgico/a a.

checkpoints: I can discuss normal meals and preferences.
I can clearly state a dietary restriction.

sections.title: Ordering in restaurants
sections.objective: Handle the main stages of a simple restaurant interaction from table request to payment.
sections.explanation: Use polite fixed chunks. Quiero is direct but possible; quisiera and me gustaría are softer. Me gusta states a preference and does not itself order an item.

patterns.form: Una mesa para dos, por favor.

patterns.meaning: What is in…? / Do you have…?

problems: Esto no es lo que he pedido. (recognition)

examples.es: Quisiera una tortilla y agua sin gas.
examples.en: I would like an omelette and still water.

examples.es: Para mí, el menú del día.

examples.en: Can you bring us the bill, please?

commonMistakes.incorrect: Me gusta un café to order
commonMistakes.explanation: Me gusta states a liking; gustaría makes the request.
No de is needed before the ordered item.

practicePrompts.prompt: Complete a restaurant dialogue: arrival, order, request and payment.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use at least five standard chunks.

practicePrompts.prompt: Say you like wine, then order a glass politely.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Me gusta el vino. Me gustaría una copa de vino.

practicePrompts.prompt: Report a missing drink and ask for it.

checkpoints: I can complete a basic restaurant interaction.
I distinguish liking, wanting and politely requesting.

sections.title: Describing areas, villages and cities
sections.objective: Describe and evaluate a neighbourhood, village or city and its facilities.
sections.explanation: Combine existence, location, adjectives and quantifiers. Give a personal evaluation with me gusta because or es + adjective.

examples.es: Es un pueblo pequeño y tranquilo.
examples.en: It is a small, quiet village.

examples.es: Hay bastantes tiendas en el centro.
examples.en: There are quite a few shops in the centre.
My neighbourhood has good transport links.

examples.es: Me gusta porque hay muchas zonas verdes.
examples.en: I like it because there are many green areas.

commonMistakes.correct: En la ciudad hay muchos museos.
commonMistakes.explanation: Hay does not take the place as its subject; introduce it with en.
Location uses estar.

practicePrompts.prompt: Give a one-minute description of your area.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use hay, está, es, a quantifier and an opinion.

practicePrompts.prompt: Compare a village and a city using simple contrasts.
Recommend an area and give two reasons.

checkpoints: I can describe facilities and overall character.
I can say where an area is and why I like/dislike it.

sections.title: Hay versus estar
sections.objective: Distinguish introducing the existence of something from locating a known, specific thing.
sections.explanation: Use hay with indefinite or quantified nouns to say what exists. Use está/están with definite, demonstrative, possessive or named subjects to say where they are.

reference.hay: Invariant in the present: hay for singular and plural.

examples.es: La farmacia está al lado del banco.
examples.en: The pharmacy is next to the bank.

examples.es: Hay dos plazas en el barrio.
examples.en: There are two squares in the neighbourhood.

commonMistakes.explanation: A definite known item is located with estar.
Present hay never changes for plural.

practicePrompts.prompt: Choose hay, está or están in ten short location sentences.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Look at the determiner and meaning.

practicePrompts.prompt: Introduce a café, then locate it.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Hay un café. El café está…

practicePrompts.prompt: Describe a room using three hay and three estar sentences.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Introduce first; refer back as definite.

checkpoints: I can explain and use the existence/location contrast.
I never pluralise present hay.

sections.title: Prepositions and place adverbs
sections.objective: Locate people, objects and places relative to landmarks.
sections.explanation: Most compound location phrases use de, which contracts with el to del. Use estar to locate a specific item.

examples.es: El móvil está encima de la mesa.
examples.en: The phone is on top of the table.

examples.es: El banco está enfrente del mercado.
examples.en: The bank is opposite the market.

examples.es: La farmacia está entre el café y la panadería.
examples.en: The pharmacy is between the café and bakery.
We live far from the centre.

commonMistakes.explanation: Cerca requires de; de + el becomes del.
Entre does not take de.

practicePrompts.prompt: Place five objects and describe their positions.
Describe the location of four places on a simple map.
Correct five phrases missing de or contractions.

checkpoints: I can use at least ten location expressions.
I form al and del automatically.

sections.title: Asking for and giving directions
sections.objective: Ask where a place is and follow or give a short route.
sections.explanation: Use polite questions for help and memorise common direction commands as chunks. At A1, intelligibility matters more than explaining the imperative system.

patterns.meaning: Excuse me, where is…? / How do you get to…?

routeChunks: está al final de la calle

examples.es: Perdone, ¿cómo se va a la estación?
examples.en: Excuse me, how do you get to the station?

examples.es: Sigue todo recto y gira a la izquierda.
examples.en: Go straight on and turn left.

examples.es: Toma la segunda calle a la derecha.
examples.en: Take the second street on the right.

examples.es: Está a unos cinco minutos a pie.
examples.en: It is about five minutes on foot.

commonMistakes.explanation: Use a before the destination; the impersonal chunk is common.
Direction uses a la derecha.

practicePrompts.prompt: Give a three-step route between two points.
Ask a stranger for the station and confirm one detail.
Follow spoken directions on a map.

checkpoints: I can ask for directions politely.
I can give and follow a route of three or four steps.

sections.title: Syllable division and word stress
sections.objective: Divide common words into syllables and place stress correctly from spelling.
sections.explanation: A written accent marks the stressed vowel. Without one, words ending in a vowel, n or s usually stress the penultimate syllable; other endings usually stress the final syllable.

reference.note: Knowing the labels is recognition-only; applying stress is active.

commonMistakes.explanation: The accent explicitly marks stress.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Giving every Spanish word penultimate stress.
commonMistakes.correct: Check the ending and written accent.
commonMistakes.explanation: Consonant endings other than n/s default to final stress.

practicePrompts.prompt: Divide ten familiar words into syllables and mark stress.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Apply accent first, then ending rule.

practicePrompts.prompt: Read a mixed list of accented and unaccented words aloud.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Exaggerate stress once, then speak naturally.

practicePrompts.prompt: Explain why café, joven and jóvenes are stressed differently.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use written accent and ending rules.

checkpoints: I can predict stress in regular written words.
I notice and respect written accent marks.

sections.title: Diphthongs and vowel combinations
sections.objective: Recognise common diphthongs so syllable division and stress remain accurate.
sections.explanation: A weak vowel i/u beside another vowel often stays in one syllable. A written accent on the weak vowel can break the pair into separate syllables (hiatus).

patterns.form: ai/ay, ei/ey, oi/oy, au, eu, ia, ie, io, ua, ue, uo
í/ú next to another vowel often creates hiatus

reference.note: Silent u in que/qui and gue/gui is not a pronounced diphthong component unless marked ü.

commonMistakes.explanation: ue forms one syllable here.
The accented weak vowel breaks the diphthong.

practicePrompts.prompt: Sort words into diphthong or hiatus.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Look for accented í/ú and pronounce aloud.

practicePrompts.prompt: Clap syllables for ten target words.
Read sentences rich in ie/ue words.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Keep the two vowels within one syllable.

checkpoints: I can hear and produce common diphthongs.
I recognise when í or ú creates a separate syllable.

sections.title: R and RR
sections.objective: Distinguish the single tap from the strong trill well enough to keep words intelligible.
sections.explanation: Single r between vowels is usually a tap. rr between vowels is strong. A single r is also strong at the beginning of a word and commonly after n, l or s.

reference.practiceAdvice: Aim first for a clear contrast; a perfect sustained trill is not required for successful communication.

commonMistakes.correct: Use a brief tongue contact for the tap.
commonMistakes.explanation: The Spanish sound is made nearer the alveolar ridge.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Writing rr at the beginning: rrestaurante.
commonMistakes.explanation: The initial single r is already pronounced strongly.

practicePrompts.prompt: Alternate pero/perro and caro/carro slowly.
Practise the strong r in syllables ra-re-ri-ro-ru, then words.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Relax and use airflow; avoid excessive tension.

practicePrompts.prompt: Record the four example phrases and compare clarity.

checkpoints: I make a perceptible tap/strong-r contrast.
I know when written r and rr represent the strong sound.
